cue: How do you say someone has what it takes?

es.meaning: To have the natural aptitude for something — to be cut out for it.
es.example: Desde joven demostró tener madera de científico.
es.exampleTranslation: Even as a boy he showed he was cut out to be a scientist.

it.meaning: To have the qualities and credentials something calls for — for the figures to add up in your favour.
it.example: Ha tutti i numeri per diventare un grande allenatore.
it.exampleTranslation: He has everything it takes to become a great coach.

bridge.note: Two ways of certifying a person before they have done anything. Italy audits you: the numbers are there, the figures add up, you meet the count — Treccani glosses it as what it takes to succeed, and lists it beside dote, pregio, requisito, titolo. Spain looks at the raw material instead: you are cut from the right timber, and madera goes back through Latin materia to mater, the source. One language checks the totals, the other checks the grain.

interference.es_to_it: The verb is the trap, and Spanish primes you straight into it. Spanish hands out DAR for this whole family — dar la talla, dar la cara — so the reach for 'dare i numeri' is almost automatic, and in Italian that means to talk nonsense, to rave, to lose the plot. Treccani files it under delirare, farneticare, vaneggiare; De Mauro adds getting furious, and, older, the dead turning up in a dream to whisper lottery numbers. Say it of a job candidate and you have called them unhinged. Then the preposition: Italian takes per + infinitive, ha i numeri PER diventare — not the Spanish de + noun.
interference.it_to_es: 'Tener los números' is nothing in Spanish. And madera needs its complement: tener madera DE + noun (madera de líder) or PARA + infinitive (madera para ser futbolista). Bare 'tiene madera' is possible but leaves the activity hanging on context. Note also the register step — RAE marks this sense colloquial, so it is a rung below avere i numeri, which is neutral enough for the exam.

review.notes: Drafted by Claude 2026-07-25. SOURCES NOT HUMAN-VERIFIED — read out of search results, so verifiedOn/verifiedBy stay null on both sides. The Treccani citation is the Sinonimi-e-Contrari page for `numero`, sense 5, which glosses the plural use as what serves for success and gives 'avere tutti i numeri'; the same entry carries 'dare i numeri' as its opposite. RAE marks madera sense 4 as coloq. — hence register colloquial and formality neutral on the ES side against standard/ok_in_exam on the IT side. NOT PAIRED WITH dar la talla, which is already banked at 0120 against essere all'altezza; 0120 is about meeting a standard, this is about innate aptitude, and the two should not be scheduled close together. FOR THE ITALIAN REVIEWER: (1) Is 'avere i numeri' equally at home outside sport and politics, where most of the attestations sit? (2) Does the bare plural need 'tutti' to sound right — avere tutti i numeri vs avere i numeri? FOR THE SPANISH REVIEWER: (1) regions set pan-regional; a WordReference thread has Argentinians offering 'tener pasta de' as the local form, so confirm madera is the one that travels. (2) Is bare 'tiene madera' natural in MX without a following de/para? CROSS-REFERENCE: the dar/avere confusion here is the third entry to hinge on Spanish DAR going somewhere Italian will not follow — 0112 (dar la cara) and 0120 (dar la talla) are the others. Worth a recurring thread.
